content.text: Seven years, mostly forgotten

The apprenticeship ran seven years, though I only remember, clearly, about seven months of it. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last.

Small gears taught me that precision and patience are, more often than not, the same virtue wearing two names. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts.

I still keep that first, over-fast movement on my own shelf now, for reasons my master would have understood. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before.

A watchmaker's apprentice learns to apologise to no one for the time a good repair takes. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud.

The loupe made the workshop's whole world the size of a coin, and I found I preferred it that size. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop.

My master called an unfinished repair a promise, and did not consider the day done until every promise was kept. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it.

A study in small gears ends, eventually, in a study of the larger, slower gear a life turns out to be. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening.

The first movement I ever finished ran eleven minutes fast a day, and I loved it anyway for being mine. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon.

A watchmaker's apprentice learns patience from gears before he learns it from people, which is the correct order. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone.

Small gears forgive nothing, my master used to say, and count that as a mercy rather than a cruelty. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely.

I spent a season on a single balance wheel and considered the season well spent. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle.

The workshop smelled of oil and brass filings, a smell I have never managed to dislike. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become.

A study in small gears is really a study in attention, dressed up in tweezers and a loupe. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits.

My master kept broken watches on a shelf as a kind of memorial to lessons he had already learned the hard way. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none.

The first movement taught me more by failing than any movement since has taught me by working. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved.

A watch that runs true is, in the end, just a very small, very patient argument won honestly. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important.

I learned to hear a bad escapement before I learned to see one, which surprised my master more than it surprised me. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it.

Gears this small do not forgive a shaking hand, so the workshop taught me stillness before it taught me skill. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.

My master's own hands shook by the end, and he taught the last lessons entirely by voice. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it.

A pocket watch carries its owner's habits in its wear pattern, if you know where on the case to look. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count.

A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome.

The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much.

A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there.

An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late.

The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down.
